Ancient Egypt

California History–Social Science 6.2

Ancient Egypt grew up along the Nile River. The Nile is a long strip of green farmland that runs through the desert. Every year the river flooded. When the water went down, it left rich black soil behind. The floods came at about the same time each year, so farmers could plan for them. At first there were two kingdoms. Upper Egypt was in the south, and Lower Egypt was in the north. Around 3100 BCE, a king named Narmer united them. Egypt's kings, later called pharaohs, ruled for about 3,000 years. Egyptians built pyramids and temples. They wrote with picture symbols called hieroglyphics. They also made a kind of paper from the papyrus plant. They believed in life after death, so they saved bodies as mummies. Famous rulers include Hatshepsut, who grew Egypt's trade, and Ramses II, a great builder. Much later, the Rosetta Stone helped people learn to read hieroglyphics again.
